s: What is the composition of the Estimates Committee, the largest financial committee of Parliament?
o: 22 members: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha
31 members: 21 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
30 members: 20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
30 members, all from the Lok Sabha
x: The Estimates Committee has 30 members, all from the Lok Sabha, with a chairman from the ruling party; the PAC has 22 (15 LS + 7 RS).

s: What is the term of office of members of the financial committees of Parliament?
x: Members are elected annually by PR-STV for a one-year term; Ministers are ineligible.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about parliamentary financial control?
o: Financial committees replace the budgetary process entirely
The budget exercises control before expenditure takes place
Financial committees exercise control after expenditure has taken place
Financial committees complement the budgetary process
x: Financial committees examine expenditure after the event and complement, rather than replace, the budgetary process.

s: How many Rajya Sabha members are associated with the Public Accounts Committee?
x: The PAC has 22 members: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha.

s: How are members of the financial committees of Parliament elected?
o: Proportional representation by single transferable vote
x: Members are elected yearly by proportional representation by single transferable vote; ministers are ineligible.

s: From which side is the chairman of the Estimates Committee invariably appointed?
x: The Estimates Committee chairman, appointed by the Speaker, is invariably from the ruling party; the PAC chair is from the Opposition.

s: Which among the following is NOT a financial committee of Parliament?
x: The three financial committees are the Estimates Committee, the PAC and COPU. The Committee on Petitions is another standing committee.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Estimates Committee has no member from the Rajya Sabha.
2. The Public Accounts Committee has 22 members.
3. Ministers can be elected to the financial committees.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The Estimates Committee has 30 members, all from the Lok Sabha; the PAC has 22 (15 + 7). Ministers are not eligible for the financial committees.

s: How many members does the Committee on Public Undertakings have?
o: 22: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha
31: 21 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
x: Like the PAC, the Committee on Public Undertakings has 22 members: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha.

s:
Match the following:
List-I (Committee)
A. Estimates Committee
B. Public Accounts Committee
C. Committee on Public Undertakings
D. Each Departmentally Related Standing Committee
List-II (Strength)
1. 22, with an Opposition chairman by convention
2. 31
3. 30, all from the Lok Sabha
4. 22, chairman chosen from its Lok Sabha members
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Estimates has 30 (all LS); PAC and COPU have 22 each, PAC chaired by the Opposition and COPU's chairman taken from its LS members; each DRSC has 31.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Public Accounts Committee?
o: A Minister can be a member of the Committee.
It has 22 members: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha.
Its members are elected annually by PR-STV.
Its Chairperson is appointed by the Speaker.
x: Ministers cannot be members of the Public Accounts Committee.

s: Which parliamentary committee has 30 members drawn from the Lok Sabha only and is the largest parliamentary committee?
x: The Estimates Committee is the largest parliamentary committee, with 30 members, all from the Lok Sabha. The PAC and Public Undertakings Committee have 22 members each.

s: For what term are members of the three Financial Committees of Parliament elected?
x: Members of the PAC, Estimates and Public Undertakings Committees are elected by PR-STV for one year.

s: How many members does the Public Accounts Committee have?
x: The PAC has 22 members, 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha; 30 from the Lok Sabha only is the Estimates Committee.

s: Which of the following is NOT a financial committee of Parliament?
o: Joint Committee on Salaries and Allowances of MPs
x: The Joint Committee on Salaries and Allowances of MPs is not a financial committee; the PAC, Estimates and COPU are.

s: How many members does the Committee on Public Undertakings have?
x: Like the PAC, the Committee on Public Undertakings has 22 members: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha.

s: From which party is the Chairman of the Estimates Committee usually appointed?
o: Any party in the Rajya Sabha
x: The Estimates Committee chair comes from the ruling party, whereas the PAC chair has come from the Opposition since 1967.

s: What does the Public Accounts Committee primarily examine?
o: Appropriation Accounts, Finance Accounts and CAG audit reports
x: The PAC examines the Appropriation Accounts, Finance Accounts and the audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor-General.

s: The Public Accounts Committee checks whether government expenditure remained within the scope of which of the following?
o: Demand for grant approved by Parliament
x: The PAC checks whether money was spent within the scope of the demand for grant approved by Parliament.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Public Accounts Committee?
o: It may take up certain matters on its own.
It tests efficiency, economy and propriety, not merely legality.
It examines the audit reports of the CAG.
It can examine the formulation of policy itself.
x: The PAC examines only the execution of policy, not policy as such; its recommendations are also not binding.

s: To whom does the Public Accounts Committee submit its reports?
x: The PAC reports to the Lok Sabha through the Speaker.

s: Why is the PAC called a 'post-mortem' check?
x: The PAC examines only the execution of policy, not policy itself, after the money is spent.

s: By convention, since 1967, from which side has the Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee been appointed?
x: Since 1967 the PAC Chairman has been an Opposition member. This is a convention, not a constitutional or statutory rule.

s: Who chaired the Public Accounts Committee of the Lok Sabha from 2010 to 2014 as an Opposition member?
x: Murli Manohar Joshi of the BJP, then in Opposition, chaired the PAC in 2010-14, following the Opposition-chair convention.

s: Which committee is described as the 'watchdog' on departmental expenditure and irregularities?
x: The PAC is the watchdog on expenditure; Petitions is the 'Ombudsman' and Estimates the 'continuous economy committee'.

s: Under which Act was the Public Accounts Committee first set up in 1921?
x: The PAC was set up in 1921 under the Government of India Act, 1919.

s: Who is the Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee for 2026-27?
x: K.C. Venugopal, an Opposition member, chairs the PAC for 2026-27, in line with the convention of an Opposition chairman. Jairam Ramesh is linked to a privilege notice; Om Birla is the Speaker; Dharmendra Pradhan is the Education Minister.

s: In which year was the Public Accounts Committee first set up?
x: The PAC was set up in 1921 under the Government of India Act, 1919; it examines the CAG's audit reports.

s: Since 1967, the Chairman of which committee has been appointed from the Opposition?
x: The Speaker has appointed the PAC Chairman from the Opposition since 1967; the Estimates Committee Chairman comes from the ruling party.

s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Estimates Committee – examination of budget estimates
Public Accounts Committee – scrutiny of public-sector undertaking accounts and commercial soundness
Estimates Committee – suggesting economy in administration
Committee on Public Undertakings – scrutiny of PSU accounts
x: The PAC scrutinises appropriation accounts and wasteful expenditure; PSU accounts are examined by the Committee on Public Undertakings.

s: What is the status of the recommendations of the Public Accounts Committee?
o: binding once approved by the Speaker
x: PAC recommendations are not binding; the PAC checks spending within the scope of the demand and examines execution, not policy.

s: Who headed the Public Accounts Committee of the 18th Lok Sabha?
x: K.C. Venugopal heads the PAC of the 18th Lok Sabha (also for 2026–27).

s: To which House does the Public Accounts Committee submit its report?
o: Both Houses in a joint sitting
Neither House; it reports to the CAG
x: The PAC reports to the Lok Sabha through the Speaker; a copy is laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha.

s: Which of the following is NOT part of the parliamentary 'watchdog' group of committees?
x: The watchdog group comprises the Committees on Subordinate Legislation and Government Assurances, the Estimates Committee, PAC, COPU and DRSCs; the Business Advisory Committee only allots time for business.

s: Which of the following committees exist only in the Lok Sabha?
o: Committee on Petitions and Committee of Privileges
Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions and Committee on Absence of Members
Rules Committee and Committee on Papers Laid on the Table
Committee on Subordinate Legislation and Committee on Government Assurances
x: The Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions and the Committee on Absence of Members are Lok Sabha-only. Petitions, Privileges, Rules, Papers Laid, Subordinate Legislation and Government Assurances committees exist in both Houses.

s: Which committee is popularly described as the ‘Ombudsman’ of Parliament?
x: The Committee on Petitions is popularly described as the Ombudsman of Parliament because it considers petitions on bills and matters of public interest.

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Committee on Government Assurances — Exercises delegated rule-making power
Business Advisory Committee — Allots time for government and other business
Committee of Privileges — Examines members’ conduct
Ethics Committee — Considers questions of privilege
x: The Business Advisory Committee allots time for government and other business. Questions of privilege belong to the Committee of Privileges, members’ conduct to the Ethics Committee, and delegated rule-making to the Committee on Subordinate Legislation.

s: Which of the following committees is chaired by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
x: The Speaker chairs the Lok Sabha Business Advisory Committee, which allots time for government and other business.

s: How many members does the Committee of Privileges of the Rajya Sabha have?
x: The Rajya Sabha Committee of Privileges has 10 members; the Lok Sabha committee has 15 nominated by the Speaker.

s: Ethics Committees were constituted in the two Houses of Parliament in which order?
o: Lok Sabha in 1997, Rajya Sabha in 2000
Rajya Sabha on 4 March 1997, Lok Sabha on 16 May 2000
Both Houses on the same day in 2000
Rajya Sabha in 2000, Lok Sabha in 2004
x: The Rajya Sabha set up its Ethics Committee first, on 4 March 1997; the Lok Sabha followed on 16 May 2000. The other options reverse or misstate the dates.

s: Which committee tracks the assurances given by ministers until they are implemented?
x: The Committee on Government Assurances tracks ministers' assurances till implemented.

s: What does the Committee on Subordinate Legislation examine?
o: The use of delegated rule-making powers
x: The Committee on Subordinate Legislation checks the use of delegated rule-making powers.

s: Which committee allots time for government and other business in the Lok Sabha?
x: The Business Advisory Committee, chaired by the Speaker, allots time for government and other business.

s: Which parliamentary committee examines the reports of the National Commissions for SCs and STs?
o: Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs
x: The Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs examines welfare programmes and the National Commissions' reports; Ministers cannot serve on it.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs:
1. Ministers cannot serve on it.
2. It examines welfare programmes for SCs and STs in Union ministries.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: ministers cannot serve on the committee, and it examines SC/ST welfare programmes in Union ministries and bodies.

s: What is the composition of the Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs?
o: 31 members: 21 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
22 members: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha
30 members: 20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
30 members, all from the Lok Sabha
x: The Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs has 30 members (20 Lok Sabha + 10 Rajya Sabha); ministers cannot serve on it.

s: Of which committee is the Speaker of the Lok Sabha the ex-officio Chairperson?
x: The Speaker is ex-officio Chairperson of the Business Advisory, Rules and General Purposes Committees.

s: How many members does the Lok Sabha Committee of Privileges have?
x: The Lok Sabha Committee of Privileges has 15 members nominated by the Speaker; the Rajya Sabha committee has 10.

s: Which parliamentary committee regulates the timetable of the House's business?
x: The Business Advisory Committee sets the timetable; the Rules Committee proposes rule changes and the Assurances Committee tracks Ministers' promises.

s: How many members does the Committee on Subordinate Legislation have in each House?
x: The Committee on Subordinate Legislation has 15 members in each House, and Ministers cannot sit on it.

s: Ministers are barred from the PAC, the Estimates Committee and the Committee on Petitions mainly because these committees:
o: consist only of Rajya Sabha members
meet only when Parliament is not in session
x: These committees, along with COPU and the Subordinate Legislation Committee, scrutinise the government, so Ministers are kept out.

s: How are committees such as the PAC, the Estimates Committee and the Committee on Public Undertakings described?
x: These committees, along with the Department-related Standing Committees, are described as watchdogs over the executive.

s: Which parliamentary committee is described as the 'Ombudsman' of Parliament, examining petitions on bills and on matters of general public interest?
x: The Committee on Petitions examines petitions on bills and matters of public interest and is called Parliament's 'Ombudsman'. The Committee on Government Assurances tracks ministers' promises, the Committee on Subordinate Legislation checks the exercise of delegated rule-making powers, and the Committee of Privileges examines breaches of privilege.

s: Who among the following cannot be a member of the Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs?
o: A member of the ruling party
x: No minister can be a member of the Committee on Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

s: In which year was the Lok Sabha Ethics Committee first constituted as an ad hoc committee?
x: It was first set up as an ad-hoc committee on 16 May 2000 and made permanent in 2015.

s: In which year was the Lok Sabha Ethics Committee made a permanent committee?
x: The Ethics Committee became permanent in 2015; it cannot take up matters pending in court.

s: Which of the following statements about the Committee on Petitions is incorrect?
o: The Lok Sabha Committee on Petitions has 15 members.
Ministers may be elected or nominated as members of the Committee on Petitions.
It examines petitions and representations submitted to the House.
The Rajya Sabha Committee on Petitions has 10 members.
x: Option B is incorrect: Ministers cannot be members of the Petitions Committee. It has 15 members in the Lok Sabha and 10 in the Rajya Sabha.

s: What does the Committee on Papers Laid on the Table primarily check?
o: The estimates contain alternative taxation policies
Public sector undertakings follow commercial principles
Papers laid by ministers, other than statutory orders, comply with the relevant requirements
x: The Committee on Papers Laid on the Table checks papers laid by ministers, other than statutory orders, for compliance.

s: Which committee examines whether Ministers' promises in the House are implemented?
o: Committee on Papers Laid on the Table
x: The Committee on Government Assurances watches Ministers' promises till they are implemented.

s: In which year was the Rajya Sabha Ethics Committee constituted?
x: The Rajya Sabha Ethics Committee was set up on 4 March 1997; the Lok Sabha had an ad hoc one in 2000, made permanent in 2015.

s: How many members does the Parliamentary Committee on the Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes have?
x: The Committee has 30 members: 20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Committee on the Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes:
1. It has 20 members from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha.
2. A Minister can be a member of this Committee.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: It has 30 members (20 LS + 10 RS) and no Minister can be a member; its chair is appointed by the Speaker.

s: In which year was the Committee on Empowerment of Women, with members from both Houses, set up?
x: The Committee on Empowerment of Women was set up for both Houses on 29 April 1997.

s: How many members does the Rajya Sabha Committee on Petitions have?
x: The Committee on Petitions has 15 members in the Lok Sabha and 10 in the Rajya Sabha.

s: Which parliamentary committee is described as a 'continuous economy committee'?
x: The Estimates Committee is called a 'continuous economy committee' because it suggests economies and alternative policies. The PAC is the 'watchdog' on expenditure; the Petitions Committee is the 'Ombudsman'; the Business Advisory Committee allots time.

s: Which parliamentary committee suggests economies and alternative policies?
x: The Estimates Committee suggests economies and alternative policies; the PAC is the watchdog on departmental expenditure and irregularities.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Committee on Public Undertakings – 1964, on the Krishna Menon Committee's recommendation
Public Accounts Committee – 1950, on John Mathai's recommendation
Departmentally Related Standing Committees – 1921, under the Government of India Act, 1919
Estimates Committee (present form) – 1993, on the Rules Committee's recommendation
x: COPU was set up in 1964 on the Krishna Menon Committee's recommendation; the PAC dates from 1921, the Estimates Committee's present form from 1950 (John Mathai) and DRSCs from 1993 (Rules Committee).

s: On whose recommendation was the Committee on Public Undertakings set up in 1964?
x: COPU came in 1964 on the Krishna Menon Committee's recommendation.

s: On whose recommendation was the Estimates Committee set up in its present form in 1950?
x: The Estimates Committee took its present form in 1950 on John Mathai's recommendation.

s: On whose recommendation was the Committee on Public Undertakings (1964) created?
x: COPU came from the Krishna Menon Committee's recommendation; John Mathai's recommendation gave the Estimates Committee its present form in 1950.

s: Which committee is described as the “Continuous economy committee”?
x: The Estimates Committee is known as the “Continuous economy committee.”

s: On whose recommendation did the Estimates Committee take its present form in 1950?
x: The Estimates Committee dates from 1921 and took its present form in 1950 on John Mathai's recommendation; Krishna Menon is linked to COPU.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: DRSCs began in 1993; the PAC dates from 1921, the Estimates Committee from 1950 and COPU from 1964.

s: The Departmentally Related Standing Committees began with 17 committees in 1993. Since which year have there been 24?
x: The DRSC system started with 17 committees in 1993 and was enlarged to 24 committees in 2004.

s: How many Department-Related Standing Committees are there in Parliament?
x: There are 24 DRSCs: 16 under the Lok Sabha and 8 under the Rajya Sabha. 22 is the strength of the PAC.

s: On whose recommendation were the Departmentally Related Standing Committees introduced in 1993?
x: DRSCs began in 1993 with 17 committees on the recommendation of the Rules Committee and became 24 from 2004.

s: What is the quorum of a Departmentally Related Standing Committee?
x: The quorum of a DRSC is 11, not 15; each DRSC has 31 members.

s: Which committees scrutinise the demands for grants, referred Bills and annual reports of the ministries under them?
x: DRSCs scrutinise demands for grants, referred Bills, annual reports and long-term policy of their ministries.

s: Of the 24 Departmentally Related Standing Committees, how many function under the Lok Sabha?
x: There are 24 DRSCs: 16 under the Lok Sabha and 8 under the Rajya Sabha.

s: How many members does each Departmentally Related Standing Committee have?
o: 30: 20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
22: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha
31: 21 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
x: Each DRSC has 31 members, 21 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha, with a quorum of 11.

s: Who appoints the Chairpersons of Department-related Standing Committees?
o: The Prime Minister for Lok Sabha committees and the Vice-President for Rajya Sabha committees
The respective ministers heading the departments concerned
The Speaker for Lok Sabha committees and the Chairman for Rajya Sabha committees
x: The Speaker appoints the Chairpersons of Lok Sabha DRSCs, while the Chairman appoints the Chairpersons of Rajya Sabha DRSCs.

s: In which year were Department-related Standing Committees (DRSCs) set up?
x: DRSCs were set up in 1993; there are 24 (16 Lok Sabha and 8 Rajya Sabha), each with 31 members and a quorum of 11.

s: How many Department-related Standing Committees are there?
x: There are 24 DRSCs, 16 under the Lok Sabha and 8 under the Rajya Sabha, each with 31 members.

s: Each Department-related Standing Committee has how many members?
x: Each DRSC has 31 members, 21 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha, with a quorum of 11.

s: How many of the 24 Department-related Standing Committees function under the Lok Sabha?
x: Of the 24 DRSCs, 16 are under the Lok Sabha and 8 under the Rajya Sabha.

s: What is a committee on a Bill made up of members of both Houses called?
x: A Joint Committee has members of both Houses and is formed on a motion; a Select Committee has members of one House only.

s: Which of the following statements regarding the 2G Spectrum Joint Parliamentary Committee is incorrect?
o: It consisted of 15 Lok Sabha members and 7 Rajya Sabha members.
It was chaired by P.C. Chacko.
It included 20 Lok Sabha members and 10 Rajya Sabha members.
x: Option B is incorrect: the 2G JPC, chaired by P.C. Chacko, had 30 members, 20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha. The 15 + 7 split belongs to the PAC.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about ad hoc committees of Parliament?
o: Inquiry committees may be set up by a motion or by the Speaker or Chairman.
The Committee on MPLADS is an example of an inquiry committee.
They continue permanently after completing their assigned task.
Select and Joint Committees on Bills are ad hoc committees.
x: Ad hoc committees end when their assigned task is completed.

s: Who constitutes Consultative Committees of MPs for particular ministries?
x: Consultative Committees are set up by the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs and are not parliamentary committees in the strict sense.

s: What is a parliamentary committee on a Bill made up of members of one House only called?
x: A Select Committee has members of one House; a Joint Committee has members of both Houses.

s: Who was the chairman of the Joint Parliamentary Committee on the 2G spectrum issue (2011)?
x: The 30-member 2G JPC (20 LS + 10 RS) was chaired by P.C. Chacko.

s: To which body was the FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026 sent in August 2026?
o: A Select Committee of the Rajya Sabha
x: The FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026 was referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee.

s: Which of the following is an ad hoc committee of Parliament?
x: Ad hoc committees are of two kinds: inquiry committees on a particular subject, and Select or Joint Committees constituted to examine Bills.

s: How is a Bill referred to a Select Committee or a Joint Committee?
o: A recommendation of the Business Advisory Committee
A decision of the Union Cabinet
x: Referral of a Bill to a Select or Joint Committee takes place through a motion in the House.

s: Inquiry committees of Parliament are examples of which type of committee?
x: Inquiry committees are ad hoc committees, not standing committees.

s: How do parliamentary committees mainly help Parliament control the administration?
o: Framing the daily agenda of the House
Undertaking detailed scrutiny that the whole House has no time for
x: Committees are a main instrument of parliamentary control, doing the detailed, complex scrutiny the whole House cannot.

s: Which of the following is an ad hoc inquiry committee of Parliament?
x: The Railway Convention Committee, like the committees on MPLADS and Security in Parliament Complex, is an ad hoc inquiry committee; the others are standing committees.

s: Before which body is the Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhisthan Bill, 2025 at present?
o: A Select Committee of the Rajya Sabha
A Select Committee of the Lok Sabha
x: The Bill is before a JPC (a joint committee of both Houses), not a single-House Select Committee.

s: In which year did a Joint Parliamentary Committee investigate the Harshad Mehta securities scam?
x: JPCs probed Bofors (1987), Harshad Mehta (1992), Ketan Parekh (2001), soft-drink pesticides (2003) and 2G spectrum (2011).

s: In which year did a Joint Parliamentary Committee investigate the Bofors issue?
x: The Bofors JPC was in 1987; Harshad Mehta 1992, Ketan Parekh 2001 and 2G spectrum 2011.

s: In which year was the JPC on the 2G spectrum issue constituted?
x: The 2G spectrum JPC was in 2011, the last of the listed scam JPCs.

s:
Match the following:
List-I (JPC on)
A. Bofors issue
B. Harshad Mehta securities scam
C. Ketan Parekh scam
D. Soft-drink pesticides
List-II (Year)
1. 2001
2. 1987
3. 2003
4. 1992
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: JPCs were set up on Bofors (1987), Harshad Mehta (1992), Ketan Parekh (2001) and soft-drink pesticides (2003).

s: Who was the chairman of the Joint Parliamentary Committee on the Bofors issue (1987)?
x: Congress leader B. Shankaranand chaired the 1987 JPC on Bofors; it reported in April 1988.

s:
Match the following:
List-I (JPC on)
A. Harshad Mehta securities scam (1992)
B. Ketan Parekh stock market scam (2001)
C. Pesticide residues in soft drinks (2003)
List-II (Chairman)
1. Sharad Pawar
2. Ram Niwas Mirdha
3. Prakash Mani Tripathi
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Ram Niwas Mirdha headed the 1992 JPC, Lt Gen Prakash Mani Tripathi (retd) the 2001 JPC, and Sharad Pawar the 2003 soft-drinks JPC.

s: Under Article 164(1A), the Council of Ministers in a State cannot exceed 15 per cent of the total strength of the Legislative Assembly, subject to what minimum?
x: The State Council of Ministers is capped at 15 per cent of the Assembly strength, but it cannot consist of fewer than 12 ministers.

s: On which date did the Anti-Defection Law (52nd Amendment) come into force?
x: The 52nd Amendment received assent on 15 February 1985 and took effect on 1 March 1985.

s: What is the main objective of the anti-defection law?
o: Ensure internal democracy within political parties
Limit the size of the Council of Ministers
Curb defections for office and promote stable governments
x: The law was meant to curb horse-trading and defections for office, promoting party discipline and stable governments.

s: The expression 'Aaya Ram Gaya Ram' became associated with defections in which State in 1967?
x: The phrase comes from Haryana, 1967; the Y.B. Chavan Committee studied defections in 1967-69, and the law came with the 52nd Amendment, 1985.

s: Whose Andhra Pradesh government was toppled by the 1984 defection led by Nadendla Bhaskara Rao?
x: Nadendla Bhaskara Rao's defection toppled N.T. Rama Rao's government in 1984; NTR was restored after a month, strengthening the demand for the 1985 law.

s: The recognition of political parties in the constitutional framework through the anti-defection provisions was introduced by which amendment and Schedule?
o: 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 and Seventh Schedule
91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 and Eleventh Schedule
44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 and Ninth Schedule
52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 and Tenth Schedule
x: Political parties entered the Constitution through the 52nd Amendment (1985), which added the Tenth Schedule on anti-defection. They were not in the original text.

s: Which Amendment added the original Tenth Schedule concerning Sikkim's association with India?
x: The 35th Amendment introduced a Sikkim-related Tenth Schedule, which the 36th Amendment omitted; it was not the anti-defection Schedule.

s: Which Articles were amended by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment (1985)?
x: The 52nd Amendment added the Tenth Schedule and amended Articles 101, 102, 190 and 191.

s: Which Amendment omitted the old Sikkim-related 'Tenth Schedule' added by the 35th Amendment (1974)?
x: The 35th Amendment's Sikkim schedule was omitted by the 36th Amendment (1975); it is not the anti-defection schedule.

s: Which committee examined the problem of defections during 1967-69?
x: The Y.B. Chavan Committee (1967-69) followed the 'Aaya Ram Gaya Ram' episode; Dinesh Goswami reported in 1990.

s: In which year did Jammu & Kashmir enact its own State anti-defection law?
x: Jammu and Kashmir passed its own anti-defection law in 1979, before the national law of 1985.

s: Which Constitutional Amendment deleted the one-third split exception and capped the Council of Ministers at 15 per cent?
x: The 91st Amendment (2003) strengthened the anti-defection law, removed the one-third split and capped the ministry at 15 per cent.

s: Under which Articles is a person disqualified for defection barred from becoming a Minister or holding a remunerative political post until re-elected?
x: Articles 75(1B), 164(1B) and 361B impose these restrictions on a disqualified defector until re-election.

s: Which Article bars a disqualified defector from holding a remunerative political post until re-elected?
x: Article 361B, added by the 91st Amendment, bars such a defector; Articles 75(1A) and 164(1A) cap the size of ministries.

s:
Consider the following statements about the 91st Constitutional Amendment, 2003:
1. It capped the Union Council of Ministers at 15 per cent of the Lok Sabha.
2. It fixed a minimum of 12 ministers in a State.
3. It deleted the merger exception under Paragraph 4.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The 91st Amendment capped ministries at 15 per cent (State minimum 12) and deleted the one-third split; the Para 4 merger exception is still in force.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the coverage of the anti-defection law?
o: Members of State Legislative Councils are covered
Nominated members are outside the scope of the law
Members of both Houses of Parliament are covered
x: Nominated members are also covered by the Tenth Schedule; they are disqualified if they join a party after six months.

s: Which one of the following is a major criticism of the anti-defection law mentioned in the context of Indian parliamentary practice?
o: It stifles intra-party dissent and legislators’ free expression without necessarily stopping mass defections.
It has abolished the Speaker’s authority over the House.
It prevents all coalition governments from being formed.
It applies exclusively to nominated Members of Parliament.
x: Critics argue that the law suppresses intra-party dissent and free expression, while failing to prevent mass defections effectively. The other statements do not describe the criticism.

s:
Assertion (A): An MP or MLA may be treated as having voluntarily given up party membership even without formally resigning.
Reason (R): Conduct such as publicly campaigning for an opposition party can constitute voluntarily giving up membership.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
x: Both are true: a member can be held to have given up party membership without resigning, because conduct such as campaigning for a rival party counts. R explains A.

s: Under the Tenth Schedule, a nominated member is disqualified if he joins a political party after how much time?
x: A nominated member may join a party within six months of taking his seat; joining after six months disqualifies him.

s: Which of the following does NOT protect a member from disqualification under the present anti-defection law?
o: Prior permission of the party for the vote
The party condoning the vote within 15 days
A split by one-third of the legislature party
A merger backed by two-thirds of the legislature party
x: The one-third split exception was deleted by the 91st Amendment (2003); prior permission, condonation within 15 days and a two-thirds merger still protect a member.

s: Under the Tenth Schedule, on which ground is an independent elected member disqualified?
o: Becomes a Minister without joining a party
Joins any political party after election
Supports the ruling side on a confidence motion
Abstains on a vote in the House
x: An independent member is disqualified only on joining a party after election; becoming a Minister without joining a party does not disqualify him.

s: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding a Presiding Officer under the Anti-Defection Law?
o: A Presiding Officer cannot rejoin the original party after demitting office.
A Presiding Officer may face disqualification for joining another political party after vacating office.
A Presiding Officer may face disqualification for joining another political party while holding office.
A Presiding Officer can voluntarily give up party membership upon election to the Chair.
x: Option A is incorrect: a presiding officer may give up party membership on election to the Chair and rejoin the party after leaving office. Joining another party, during or after the term, disqualifies them.

s: Voting or abstaining contrary to the party whip without prior permission is a ground of disqualification under which paragraph of the Tenth Schedule?
x: Defying the whip is covered by Para 2(1)(b); Para 4 is the merger exception, Para 5 concerns presiding officers and Para 6 the deciding authority.

s: Under Paragraph 5 of the Tenth Schedule, on which ground is a Presiding Officer disqualified?
o: Leaves his party on election to the office
Rejoins his party after vacating office
Remains a member of his party while in office
x: Para 5 lets a Presiding Officer leave his party on election and rejoin after office; joining another party disqualifies him.

s: Within how many days may a political party condone a member's vote against its whip, so that the member is not disqualified?
x: Under the Tenth Schedule, a member who votes or abstains against the whip is not disqualified if the party condones it within 15 days.

s: Why has the two-thirds rule under Paragraph 4 of the Tenth Schedule been criticised?
o: Protect individual dissent against the whip
x: The Paragraph 4 two-thirds rule has been used as a defence for mass defection and so attracts criticism.

s: Under Para 4 of the Tenth Schedule, what is required for protection from disqualification on the ground of merger?
o: two-thirds of the legislature party agrees to merge and the original political party also merges
all members of the legislature party join another party
one-half of the legislature party joins another party
the Speaker alone approves the merger
x: A valid merger requires two conditions: the original political party must merge with another party, and at least two-thirds of the legislature party must agree to the merger.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about parliamentary privileges?
o: Article 105 protects freedom of speech in Parliament
Article 194 protects freedom of speech in State Legislatures
Privileges are fully codified in a single parliamentary statute
Privileges also rest on conventions, rules, statutes and judicial rulings
x: Parliamentary privileges have never been codified in a single statute; they rest on conventions, rules, statutes and court rulings. Articles 105 and 194 give the speech protection.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 105 – Courts not to inquire into proceedings of Parliament
x: Article 194 deals with State Legislature privileges; Article 105 with Parliament's privileges, Article 122 with parliamentary proceedings and Article 212 with State Legislature proceedings.

s: In Raja Ram Pal (2007), what did the Supreme Court hold about decisions of a House in matters of privilege?
o: Reviewable only for gross illegality or unconstitutionality
Reviewable on every ground of procedural irregularity
Subject to approval by the President
x: Raja Ram Pal (2007) held that privilege decisions can be reviewed, but only for gross illegality or unconstitutionality. They are not wholly immune; mere procedural irregularity is protected by Art. 122/212; the President has no approving role.

s: Under which rules does a Member of Parliament generally raise a breach of privilege or contempt by a minister, another member or an outsider?
o: Lok Sabha Rule 187 or Rajya Sabha Rule 222
Lok Sabha Rule 222 or Rajya Sabha Rule 187
x: Privilege notices are raised under Rule 222 in the Lok Sabha and Rule 187 in the Rajya Sabha, usually after Question Hour.

s: In a breach of privilege case, who takes the final decision on action against the offender?
x: The Committee of Privileges examines and recommends, but the House takes the final decision.

s: Which of the following best distinguishes contempt of the House from breach of privilege?
o: Contempt is wider and includes any act obstructing the House or its members in their functions
Contempt is narrower and concerns only members of the House
Breach of privilege applies only to ministers, whereas contempt applies only to outsiders
There is no distinction between the two expressions
x: Contempt has a wider scope and includes acts that obstruct the House or its members in the discharge of their functions. A breach concerns infringement of a specific privilege.

s: What is the composition of the Committee of Privileges of the Rajya Sabha?
o: 10 members usually chaired by the Deputy Chairman
22 members chaired by the Leader of the Opposition
31 members chaired by a member of the ruling party
x: The Rajya Sabha Privileges Committee has 10 members and is usually chaired by the Deputy Chairman. Fifteen members is the Lok Sabha committee's strength; 22 and 31 are PAC/COPU and DRSC sizes.

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 75(1A) — Fifteen per cent limit on the Union Council of Ministers
Para 3 of the Tenth Schedule — Split exception
Para 4 of the Tenth Schedule — Merger exception
Article 105(1)-(2) — Fifteen per cent limit on a State Council of Ministers
x: Article 105(1)-(2) concerns freedom of speech and related parliamentary privileges. The 15 per cent limit on a State Council of Ministers is provided under Article 164(1A).

s: What did the Supreme Court hold about legislative privilege in Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024)?
o: gives no immunity for bribery connected with speaking or voting
gives complete immunity for accepting a bribe to speak or vote
applies only to proceedings of State Legislatures
overrides the power of courts to investigate corruption
x: The seven-judge Bench held that privilege does not protect bribery to speak or vote, thereby overruling the contrary position in P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998).

s: Which Article bars courts from questioning proceedings of Parliament on the ground of procedural irregularity?
x: Article 122 protects proceedings of Parliament from court inquiry for procedural irregularity; Article 212 does the same for State Legislatures.

s: The Committee of Privileges of the Lok Sabha consists of how many members nominated by the Speaker?
x: The Lok Sabha Privileges Committee has 15 members nominated by the Speaker; the Rajya Sabha committee has 10.

s: Which earlier judgment did the seven-judge Bench of the Supreme Court overrule in Sita Soren (2024)?
x: Sita Soren held there is no immunity for bribery to speak or vote, overruling P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998).

s: Which of the following punishments can a House of Parliament impose on a person found guilty of breach of privilege or contempt?
x: The House can punish by admonition, reprimand, imprisonment, or suspension or expulsion of a member.

s: Who can be punished by a House of Parliament for breach of its privileges?
x: Breach of privilege or contempt can be committed by members as well as outsiders, and both can be punished by the House.

s: In which kind of cases does the freedom from arrest of Members of Parliament apply?
o: Civil, criminal and preventive detention cases
x: Freedom from arrest covers only civil cases; it does not apply to criminal cases or preventive detention.

s: For how many days before and after a session of the House do members enjoy freedom from arrest in civil cases?
x: Members cannot be arrested in civil cases during a session and for 40 days before and after it.

s: Which of the following is a collective privilege of a House of Parliament, and not an individual privilege of its members?
o: Freedom from arrest in civil cases
Right to receive immediate information of the arrest of a member
Right to decline to give evidence in a court while the House is in session
x: The right to be informed at once of a member's arrest, detention or release belongs to the House; the other three are privileges of individual members.

s: Which of the following is NOT an individual privilege of a Member of Parliament?
o: Freedom of speech in the House
Freedom from arrest in civil cases during a session
Right to exclude strangers from the sittings of the House
x: Excluding strangers from its sittings is a collective privilege of the House; the others are privileges of individual members.

s: Which Article deals with disqualifications for membership of a State Legislature?
x: Article 191 covers State disqualifications and 190 State vacation of seats; Articles 101 and 102 are the Parliament counterparts.

s: Which Articles govern defection disqualification of Members of Parliament and State Legislatures, respectively?
x: Defection disqualification comes under Article 102(2) for MPs and 191(2) for State legislators, read with the Tenth Schedule. Clauses (1) are the general grounds.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about general (non-defection) disqualification of legislators?
o: The President decides the question for a Union MP.
The Governor decides the question for a State MLA or MLC.
The ECI's opinion is non-binding in the case of a State legislator.
The ECI's opinion is mandatory and binding in the case of an MP.
x: For both MPs and State legislators the ECI's opinion is compulsory and binding.

s: Who decides the general (non-defection) disqualification of a Member of Parliament?
o: Speaker or Chairman of the House
x: General disqualification of an MP is decided by the President (on the Election Commission's binding opinion); defection cases go to the Speaker or Chairman.

s: In what capacity does the Speaker or Chairman act while deciding a disqualification question under the Tenth Schedule?
x: The presiding officer acts as a tribunal, subject to limited judicial review; the ECI gives no opinion here (that applies under Articles 103 and 192).

s: Why was Paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule struck down in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu?
o: It barred judicial review without the required ratification by the States under Article 368(2)
It transferred disqualification powers to the Election Commission
It permitted nominated members to vote in all elections
It abolished the office of the Speaker
x: Paragraph 7 attempted to oust the jurisdiction of courts. Its provisions were held invalid because the amendment had not been ratified by the States as required under Article 368(2).

s: When is judicial review of a decision of the Speaker or Chairman under the Tenth Schedule generally available?
o: under no circumstances, because the decision is final
before the decision is made, on every question of fact
only after the decision, and on limited grounds such as mala fides or perversity
only when the Election Commission grants permission
x: Kihoto Hollohan preserved judicial review after the decision, but limited it to grounds such as mala fides, perversity, violation of natural justice and constitutional mandate.

s: What time limit does the Tenth Schedule prescribe for the Presiding Officer to decide a defection petition?
x: The Tenth Schedule sets no time limit for deciding a defection petition, which is often criticised.

s: What is the role of the Election Commission's opinion in defection disqualification cases under the Tenth Schedule?
x: The Election Commission gives no opinion in defection cases; its opinion is binding only in general disqualification cases decided by the President or Governor.

s: In July 2026, what did the Bench of Justices P.S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe say about the shortcomings of Paragraph 4?
o: Outside the jurisdiction of every constitutional authority
Matters for the Election Commission alone
x: The Bench sought the Centre’s reply but observed that any shortcomings in Paragraph 4 were matters for Parliament.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about anti-defection case law?
o: G. Viswanathan: an expelled member continues to belong to the original party for Tenth Schedule purposes.
G. Viswanathan: expulsion automatically protects a member from disqualification for joining another party.
G. Viswanathan: an expelled member who joins another party may be treated as having voluntarily given up membership.
Ravi S. Naik: voluntarily giving up membership may be inferred from conduct.
x: Expulsion gives no such protection; an expelled member who joins another party may be disqualified for voluntarily giving up membership.

s: In the Karnataka defection case (2019), the Supreme Court upheld the disqualification of how many rebel MLAs?
x: The Court upheld the disqualification of 17 rebel MLAs but held the Speaker could not bar them from contesting till the end of the term.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992)?
o: It was decided by a Constitution Bench.
It upheld the constitutional validity of the Tenth Schedule.
It struck down Paragraph 7 of the Schedule.
It held that the Tenth Schedule violates the basic structure by restricting legislators' freedom of speech.
x: The Court held that the law did not violate legislators' freedom of speech or the basic structure.

s: In Keisham Meghachandra Singh v. Speaker, Manipur, within what time did the Supreme Court say disqualification petitions should ordinarily be decided?
x: The Supreme Court indicated that the Speaker should decide disqualification petitions within three months, except in extraordinary circumstances.

s: In Keisham Meghachandra Singh v. Speaker, Manipur, with what did the Supreme Court ask Parliament to consider replacing the Speaker in defection cases?
x: The Court suggested a permanent independent tribunal; it did not transfer Tenth Schedule decisions to the Election Commission.

s: According to the Subhash Desai judgment, who appoints the whip of a party in the House?
x: The legislature party cannot be conflated with the political party, and it is the political party that appoints the whip.

s: Which pair of case and holding is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Ravi S. Naik v. Union of India – voluntarily giving up membership may be inferred from conduct
G. Viswanathan v. Speaker, Tamil Nadu – expelled member continues to belong to the party
Subhash Desai v. Principal Secretary, Governor of Maharashtra – expelled member continues to belong to the party
Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu – upheld the validity of the Tenth Schedule
x: Subhash Desai held that the political party appoints the whip and the leader in the House; the expelled-member holding is G. Viswanathan.

s: In the Telangana Speaker matter, how much time did the Supreme Court later allow for deciding the last two of ten BRS disqualification petitions?
x: After a time-bound direction, the Supreme Court gave three weeks for the last two of ten BRS petitions, warning of contempt.

s: Which case held that voluntarily giving up party membership is different from resigning and can be inferred from conduct?
x: Ravi S. Naik (1994) held that giving up membership can be inferred from conduct; G. Viswanathan dealt with expelled members.

s: In G. Viswanathan (1996), what did the Supreme Court hold about a member expelled from his party?
o: Is free to join any other party
x: An expelled member still belongs to his party; if he joins another party, he is treated as having given up membership.

s: Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) was decided by what majority?
x: Kihoto Hollohan upheld the Tenth Schedule and struck down Para 7 by a 3:2 majority.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Subhash Desai judgment (May 2023)?
o: The political party appoints the whip
The political party appoints the leader in the House
Legislators alone can bring about a 'deemed merger'
The legislature party does not override the political party
x: Subhash Desai held that the political party, not the legislature party, appoints the whip and leader, and that legislators alone cannot create a deemed merger.

s: In the Karnataka defection case (2019), what did the Supreme Court hold that the Speaker cannot do?
o: Disqualify rebels for giving up membership
Bar the disqualified MLAs from contesting elections
x: The Court upheld the disqualification of 17 rebels but held that the Speaker cannot bar them from contesting.

s: Why is delay by Speakers in deciding disqualification petitions a concern?
o: Speakers need the Governor's approval to decide
The Election Commission must concur in every decision
Petitions must first be heard by the High Court
There is no fixed time limit and Speakers remain members of their parties
x: There is no fixed time limit, and Speakers, who do not resign from their parties, decide petitions in a partisan context.

s: In April 2026, seven Rajya Sabha MPs of which party joined the BJP, an episode cited as misuse of the merger exception?
x: Seven AAP Rajya Sabha MPs joined the BJP in April 2026; twenty TMC MPs joining the NPCI in June 2026 was the other example cited.

s: What was the constitutional significance of the June 2019 event involving four of the six TDP Rajya Sabha MPs?
o: They were disqualified by the Rajya Sabha Chairman for voting against the party
They were nominated to the Rajya Sabha by the President
They merged with the BJP under Paragraph 4, and the Rajya Sabha Chairman accepted the merger
They formed an independent party without invoking the Tenth Schedule
x: In June 2019, four of the six TDP Rajya Sabha MPs were treated as having merged with the BJP under Paragraph 4, and the Rajya Sabha Chairman accepted the merger.

s: What does 'resort politics' refer to in the context of anti-defection and floor tests?
o: Sending legislators abroad for parliamentary training
Dissolving the legislature before a confidence motion
Sequestering legislators before a floor test to prevent poaching
Suspending legislators who abstain from voting
x: Resort politics involves keeping legislators together or sequestered before a floor test to prevent rival parties from poaching them.

s: What do legislators do in the 'resignation route' used to avoid disqualification proceedings?
o: Seek prior permission from the Election Commission before switching parties
Resign, lowering the majority mark, and later re-contest on the new party's ticket
Abstain from every vote until the next election
Merge into the new party without resigning
x: In the resignation route, MLAs resign instead of defecting, reducing the majority mark without disqualification, and may re-contest on the new party's ticket.

s: What happened to the disqualification petitions against 23 YSRCP MLAs who moved to the TDP between 2014 and 2019?
o: Upheld, and the MLAs disqualified immediately
Decided by the Supreme Court in 2014
x: The petitions were never decided, a standard example of delay by the Speaker in anti-defection proceedings.

s: Which of the following is a newer proposal concerning the anti-defection law?
o: Exempting independent members from the law
Fixed timelines for Speakers and an independent tribunal
x: Newer proposals include fixed constitutional timelines for Speakers and an independent tribunal, the latter suggested for consideration by the Supreme Court in 2020.

s: Which body (1990) recommended disqualification only for voluntarily giving up membership or defying the whip on a confidence motion?
x: The Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) made this recommendation; the Law Commission's 170th Report (1999) recommended deleting the split and merger exceptions.

s: What does the proposal to limit the whip and disqualification under the anti-defection law to confidence and money votes seek to ensure for legislators?
o: Vote against every money bill without party discipline
Avoid all party whips during the entire legislative term
Dissent even on a confidence motion without consequences
Dissent freely on matters that do not threaten the government's survival
x: The proposal would retain party discipline for votes threatening government survival, such as confidence, no-confidence and money bills, while allowing dissent on other matters.

s:
Arrange the following reform proposals in chronological order:
A. Law Commission’s 170th Report
B. Dinesh Goswami Committee recommendation
C. Manish Tewari’s private member’s Bill
D. Supreme Court suggestion to consider an independent tribunal
x: The sequence is Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990), Law Commission’s 170th Report (1999), Manish Tewari’s Bill (2010), and the Supreme Court’s independent-tribunal suggestion (2020).

s: Which body recommended that the vote cast by a defector be treated as invalid?
x: The NCRWC (2002) recommended that defectors be barred from office and their votes treated as invalid.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Manish Tewari Bill – deleting the split and merger exceptions
Law Commission (170th Report) – pre-poll alliances to be treated as parties
NCRWC – limiting the law to confidence and money votes
Dinesh Goswami Committee – defector's vote to be invalid
x: The Law Commission's 170th Report wanted pre-poll alliances treated as parties; the Manish Tewari Bill sought to limit the law to confidence and money votes.

s: In which of the following was the proposal to limit the anti-defection law to confidence and money votes made?
x: The Manish Tewari Bill (2010) proposed limiting the law to confidence and money votes so members could dissent freely elsewhere.

s: Which body recommended deleting both the split and the merger exceptions of the Tenth Schedule and treating pre-poll alliances as parties?
x: The Law Commission's 170th Report (1999) recommended deleting the split and merger provisions and treating pre-poll alliances as parties.

s: In which year was the Leader of Opposition first formally recognized?
x: The Leader of the Opposition was first formally recognised in 1969.

s: Under which Act is statutory status given to the Leader of the Opposition?
o: Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977
x: The Leader of the Opposition has statutory status under the Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977.

s: Since which year has the Public Accounts Committee generally been chaired by a member of the Opposition?
x: The Public Accounts Committee has been chaired by a member of the Opposition since 1967.

s: What numerical threshold must the largest opposition party meet for recognition as the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha?
o: At least 5% of the total House strength
At least 15% of the total House strength
At least 10% of the total House strength
At least 20% of the total House strength
x: To be recognised as Leader of the Opposition, the largest opposition party needs at least 10% of the House, about 55 Lok Sabha seats.

s: Who was the first Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha recognised under the Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977?
x: Y.B. Chavan was the first Leader of the Opposition recognised under the 1977 Act; the APPSC 2002 key also gave Y.B. Chavan.

s: In which Lok Sabha was the highest share of Bills referred to parliamentary committees?
x: The 15th Lok Sabha referred 71% of Bills to committees, against 60% in the 14th, 25% in the 16th and only 16% in the 17th.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: India – more than half of Bills referred to committees
India – less than one-fifth of Bills referred to committees
United Kingdom – only Money Bills examined by committees
United Kingdom – Bills examined by committees of one House only
x: Less than one-fifth of Indian Bills go to committees, while every UK Bill is examined by committees of both Houses.

s: In which year was the system of Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees introduced in India?
x: The systematic committee system, including Department-related Standing Committees, began in 1993.

s: What share of Bills was referred to parliamentary committees in the Seventeenth Lok Sabha?
x: Only 16 per cent of Bills were referred in the 17th Lok Sabha, against 71 per cent in the 15th.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Seventeenth Lok Sabha:
1. 58 per cent of Bills were passed within two weeks.
2. 71 per cent of Bills were referred to committees.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: 58 per cent of Bills passed within two weeks; only 16 per cent were referred (71 per cent was the 15th Lok Sabha).

s: In the light of which Supreme Court case was it proposed that courts test the urgency of ordinances?
x: The proposals included judicial examination of urgency in light of Krishna Kumar Singh (2017), defining 'immediate necessity' and publishing reasons.

s: What is the main constitutional concern about the use of the Money Bill route?
o: Requires the approval of every State Legislature
Can bypass the Rajya Sabha for measures that may not strictly fall within Article 110
Can be introduced only in the Rajya Sabha
Prevents the Lok Sabha from considering financial legislation
x: The Money Bill route may bypass the Rajya Sabha for laws whose provisions may not strictly fit within Article 110. The Aadhaar Act, 2016, is cited as an example.

s: Through which route is the Aadhaar Act, 2016 cited as an example of bypassing the Rajya Sabha?
x: The Money Bill route (Article 110) bypasses the Rajya Sabha for laws not strictly fitting it, such as the Aadhaar Act, 2016.

s: The ordinance route of law-making is based on which Article?
x: Ordinances are issued under Article 123; Article 110 defines Money Bills.

s: In the 17th Lok Sabha, what proportion of Bills were referred to parliamentary committees?
x: Only 16% of Bills in the 17th Lok Sabha were referred to committees; the corresponding figure for the 15th Lok Sabha was 71%.

s: What share of Bills was referred to parliamentary committees in the 15th Lok Sabha?
x: 71% of Bills went to committees in the 15th Lok Sabha, against only 16% in the 17th.

s: The First Lok Sabha sat for about how many days a year on average?
x: Average sittings fell from about 135 days a year in the First Lok Sabha to about 55 in the Seventeenth (2019-24).

s: The Lok Sabha generally sits for about how many days in a year?
x: The Lok Sabha sits around 60–70 days a year, whereas the UK House of Commons has more than 150 sittings.

s: What does Article 85(1) of the Constitution provide?
o: The Rajya Sabha must sit for at least 100 days every year
There cannot be a gap of more than six months between two sessions of Parliament
The Lok Sabha must hold three sessions every year
Parliament must sit for at least 120 days every year
x: Article 85(1) bars a gap of more than six months between sessions but prescribes no minimum number of sitting days.

s: In the Seventeenth Lok Sabha, Question Hour ran for approximately what proportion of its scheduled time?
x: During the Seventeenth Lok Sabha, Question Hour ran for only 60 per cent of its scheduled time.

s: According to PRS, what was the productivity of the Lok Sabha in the Monsoon Session of 2026?
x: PRS placed Lok Sabha productivity at 19 per cent and Rajya Sabha productivity at 39 per cent in the Monsoon Session of 2026.

s: The UK House of Commons sits for about how many days a year?
x: The Lok Sabha now sits 60-70 days a year against 150 or more in the UK House of Commons.

s: In the Monsoon Session of 2026, the Lok Sabha's Question Hour ran for what share of its scheduled time?
x: Question Hour ran only 1 per cent of scheduled time in the Lok Sabha and 12 per cent in the Rajya Sabha.

s: According to PRS, what was the productivity of the Rajya Sabha in the Monsoon Session of 2026?
x: PRS put Rajya Sabha productivity at 39 per cent in the Monsoon Session 2026, against 19 per cent for the Lok Sabha.

s: Which Article bars a gap of more than six months between two sessions of a State Legislature?
x: Article 174 sets the six-month rule for State Legislatures; PRS found many Assemblies met only to satisfy it.

s: On how many occasions have joint sittings of Parliament been held so far?
x: Joint sittings of Parliament have been used only three times so far.

s: In the 17th Lok Sabha, for about what share of its scheduled time did Question Hour function?
x: In the 17th Lok Sabha, Question Hour ran for only about 60% of its time.

s: Which Lok Sabha rule provides for automatic suspension of a member for grave disorder?
x: Rule 374A provides automatic suspension for grave disorder; Rule 373 only directs a member to withdraw for the day.

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Rajya Sabha Rule 255 — suspension by House motion for the remainder of the session
Lok Sabha Rule 373 — withdrawal for the day ordered by the Speaker
Lok Sabha Rule 374 — suspension by House motion
Rajya Sabha Rule 256 — suspension by House motion, not beyond the remainder of the session
x: Rule 255 of the Rajya Sabha authorises the Chairman to direct withdrawal for the day. Suspension by House motion is dealt with under Rule 256.

s: Which Rajya Sabha rule provides for suspension of a member by a House motion, not beyond the session?
x: Rule 256 is the Rajya Sabha's House-motion suspension rule; Rule 255 only directs withdrawal for the day.

s: For how long does automatic suspension of a Lok Sabha member under Rule 374A last?
o: Five sittings or the rest of the session
The rest of the Lok Sabha's term
x: Rule 374A suspends a member automatically for five sittings or the rest of the session, whichever is less.

s: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Rule 373 – Lok Sabha member withdraws for the day
Rule 255 – Rajya Sabha member withdraws for the day
Rule 374 – Lok Sabha suspension by House motion
Rule 256 – automatic suspension in the Rajya Sabha
x: Rule 256 provides suspension by a House motion; automatic suspension exists only under Lok Sabha Rule 374A.

s: In 2012 the Union Parliamentary Affairs Minister put the cost of running Parliament at about how much per minute?
x: In 2012 Pawan Kumar Bansal said each minute of Parliament costs about Rs 2.5 lakh; this figure is still used to value time lost to disruptions.

s: What minimum annual sitting days did the NCRWC recommend?
o: 150 for Lok Sabha and 120 for Rajya Sabha
120 for Lok Sabha and 100 for Rajya Sabha
100 for Lok Sabha and 120 for Rajya Sabha
x: The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution recommended 120 sitting days for Lok Sabha and 100 for Rajya Sabha.

s: Which of the following is NOT a proposal for improving parliamentary functioning?
o: Restricting all opposition debate to confidence motions alone
Making committee scrutiny mandatory before passage of Bills
x: The proposals include a fixed calendar, stronger Question Hour, mandatory committee scrutiny, and protection of opposition debate time. The proposal is to limit whips, not all opposition debate, to confidence votes and Money Bills.

s: What is the proposed National Legislative Index meant to assess?
o: Only the attendance of Members of Parliament
Sittings, legislative business, disruptions, committee use and grievance redressal
The performance of State courts and tribunals
Only the financial expenditure of Parliament
x: The National Legislative Index covers sittings, business, disruptions, use of committees and grievance redressal.

s: According to Digital Sansad data, what was the attendance at meetings of Department-related Standing Committees?
x: Digital Sansad, the Lok Sabha website, gives official attendance data such as 53 per cent at DRSC meetings.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: PRS Legislative Research – session productivity and reviews of State laws
Digital Sansad – minimum 120 sitting days for the Lok Sabha
NCRWC – official attendance data of MPs
National Legislative Index – announced by the Rajya Sabha Chairman
x: PRS tracks session productivity, Bill scrutiny and State-law reviews; the National Legislative Index was announced by the Lok Sabha Speaker.

s: Who chaired the Business Advisory Committee that fixed the agenda for the Budget Session 2026 of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly?
x: The Business Advisory Committee fixing the agenda was chaired by Speaker Chintakayala Ayyanna Patrudu.

s: The proposed enlargement of the Lok Sabha would raise its strength from 550 to how many?
x: The proposal raises the Lok Sabha from 550 to 850 seats, taking the Lok Sabha–Rajya Sabha ratio from 2.2:1 to 3.3:1.

s: Where was the 86th All India Presiding Officers' Conference (AIPOC) held?
x: The 86th AIPOC was held at Lucknow with the theme 'Strong Legislature - Prosperous Nation'.

s: As per the PRS Review of State Laws 2025, State Assemblies met on average for about how many days?
x: State Assemblies met for an average of 24 days, ranging from 43 in Odisha to 7 in Nagaland.

s: When was the Budget Session 2026 of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly held?
x: The AP Budget Session 2026 ran from 11 February to 7 March 2026, with the agenda fixed by the BAC chaired by the Speaker.

s: Since which year has the All India Presiding Officers' Conference (AIPOC) been held?
x: AIPOC dates from 1921; its 86th session was held at Lucknow.

s: As per the PRS Review of State Laws 2025, which State Assembly met for the highest number of days?
x: Assemblies met for an average of 24 days; Odisha met the most (43 days) and Nagaland the least (7).

s: Which Constitution Amendment Bill proposes to raise the strength of the Lok Sabha from 550 to 850?
x: The 131st Amendment Bill proposes a Lok Sabha of 850, changing the Lok Sabha to Rajya Sabha ratio from 2.2:1 to 3.3:1.

s: As per the PRS Review of State Laws 2025, which State Assembly met for the fewest days?
x: Assemblies met on average for 24 days; Odisha met the most (43) and Nagaland the fewest (7).

s: What was the theme of the 86th All India Presiding Officers' Conference held at Lucknow?
x: The 86th AIPOC at Lucknow had the theme 'Strong Legislature - Prosperous Nation'.

s: Under Article 74(1), why does the President ordinarily act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers?
o: the Council of Ministers is responsible to the Rajya Sabha
the advice of the Council of Ministers is constitutionally binding
the Prime Minister is directly elected by the people
the President is the de facto executive
x: Article 74(1) provides for a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President, and the President is bound by that advice.

s: In the Indian parliamentary system, who provides central leadership to the Council of Ministers?
x: The Prime Minister leads the Council of Ministers; the President is only the nominal head of the executive.

s: Who is the Leader of the Lok Sabha (Leader of the House) and the chief spokesperson of the Government?
x: The Prime Minister leads the majority in the Lok Sabha, is Leader of the House and the Government's chief spokesperson; the President is Head of State.

s: In the Indian parliamentary system, to whom are ministers individually responsible?
x: Ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75) and individually responsible to the President.

s: Which Article provides for the collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha?
x: Article 75 makes the Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha; Article 74(1) makes advice binding on the President.

s: Within how many months must a minister who is not a Member of Parliament become one, or cease to be a minister?
x: Under dual membership, a non-member may be a minister for up to six months; he must enter Parliament within that time.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Parliamentary system – fixed tenure, removable only by impeachment
Parliamentary system – executive responsible to the legislature
x: Responsibility of the executive to the legislature is the defining test of a parliamentary system, which is why India is parliamentary.

s: By which other names is the parliamentary form of government also known?
x: The parliamentary system is also called cabinet government or responsible government, since it stays in power only while it has a majority in the popular House.

s: On which principle is the parliamentary system of government based?
o: Fusion of executive and legislative powers
x: The parliamentary system rests on fusion of executive and legislative powers, while the presidential system rests on separation of powers.

s: Which of the following is a feature of the presidential system?
o: A plural executive headed by a Prime Minister
Executive accountable to the legislature as in a parliamentary system
A fixed term for the executive
Fusion of executive and legislative powers
x: A presidential system generally has a single, directly elected executive with a fixed term, not accountable to the legislature in the parliamentary sense.

s: In a semi-presidential system, to whom is the Prime Minister responsible?
x: In a semi-presidential system a President and a Prime Minister coexist; the President may have real powers, while the Prime Minister is responsible to the legislature.

s: Which one of the following sets contains only examples of parliamentary systems?
o: United Kingdom, Japan, Canada and India
United States, Brazil, India and Canada
United Kingdom, United States, Brazil and Japan
Brazil, United States, Canada and India
x: The United Kingdom, Japan, Canada and India are examples of parliamentary systems. The United States and Brazil are presidential systems.

s: Which of the following countries are associated with semi-presidential systems in which a President and a Prime Minister coexist?
o: Sri Lanka, the United Kingdom and the United States
Russia, India and the United States
India, the United Kingdom and France
x: France, Russia and Sri Lanka are identified as examples of countries where a President and a Prime Minister coexist under a semi-presidential arrangement.

s: In which year was France's Fifth Republic established?
x: France's Fifth Republic dates from 1958.

s: In which year was Sri Lanka's semi-presidential Constitution adopted?
x: Sri Lanka's semi-presidential Constitution dates from 1978; France's Fifth Republic from 1958.

s: Which of the following countries does NOT have a semi-presidential system?
x: India's President is indirectly elected and nominal, so India is not semi-presidential, unlike France, Russia and Sri Lanka.

s: Which of the following features is associated with Britain but not with India in the same form?
o: Collective responsibility to the lower House
x: Britain has an institutionalised shadow cabinet, legal ministerial responsibility and ministers who must be MPs; India lacks these in the same form.

s: In India, to what is the removal of the Prime Minister's government linked?
o: A decision of the ruling party
x: In India, removal is linked to losing the confidence of the Lok Sabha, whereas in the UK the ruling party can replace its Prime Minister.

s: In which country did the Westminster model of parliamentary government originate?
x: The parliamentary system originated in Britain and is commonly called the Westminster model.

s: In Britain, from which House is the Prime Minister drawn?
x: The British Prime Minister is drawn from the House of Commons; in India the Prime Minister may belong to either House.

s: Which of the following applies to the Indian Parliament but not to the British Parliament?
o: Hereditary monarch as head of state
Subject to the basic structure doctrine
x: The basic structure doctrine belongs to the Indian constitutional framework; sovereignty of Parliament, a hereditary monarch and the shadow cabinet are British.

s: The British system rests on sovereignty of Parliament. On what does the Indian system rest?
x: India has a written Constitution and constitutional supremacy; Britain has sovereignty of Parliament.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Indian and British systems:
1. India's Head of State is indirectly elected for five years.
2. British courts can strike down Acts of Parliament.
3. Britain's Constitution is unwritten.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: India's President is indirectly elected for five years and Britain's Constitution is unwritten; British courts cannot question Acts of Parliament.

s: In India, from which House of Parliament can the Prime Minister be drawn?
x: In India the Prime Minister may be a member of either House, whereas in Britain the Prime Minister comes from the House of Commons.

s: Which of the following features is found in the British system but not in the Indian system?
o: Collective responsibility to the lower House
Prime Minister as leader of the majority party
x: In Britain ministers are legally responsible (a minister must countersign acts of the Crown); India has no such legal responsibility of ministers.

s: On what is judicial review based in India and in the USA, respectively?
o: Due process of law; procedure established by law
Procedure established by law; due process of law
Due process of law in both
Procedure established by law in both
x: India follows the narrower 'procedure established by law', while the USA follows the wider 'due process of law' standard.

s: In which year did the United States adopt the 22nd Amendment, associated with limiting presidential tenure?
x: The US adopted the 22nd Amendment in 1951; India has no term limit for its Prime Minister.

s: In the USA, in whom are the residuary powers of legislation vested?
x: Residuary powers lie with the States in the USA and with Parliament (the Union) in India.

s: Which of the following is NOT common to India and the USA?
o: Residuary powers vested in the States
x: Residuary powers lie with the States only in the USA; in India they lie with the Union. The other three are common.

s: On 22 March 2026, Narendra Modi passed whose record as the longest-serving head of an elected government?
x: Modi completed 8,931 days, passing Pawan Kumar Chamling's 8,930; India has no term limit for the PM, unlike the US 22nd Amendment.

s: Because of its wide power of judicial review, which country's Supreme Court has been called a 'third chamber' of the legislature?
x: The US Supreme Court uses 'due process of law' and has wide judicial review, so it is called a 'third chamber'.

s: Which of the following is a demerit of the presidential system?
o: Frequent fall of governments through no-confidence motions
x: Executive-legislature deadlock (and a personality cult around a single executive) are demerits of the presidential system; it has a fixed tenure.

s: 'Cabinet dictatorship' with a large majority is a demerit of which system?
x: Cabinet dictatorship under a large majority is listed as a demerit of the parliamentary system; deadlock and personality cult are presidential demerits.

s: Which of the following is a merit of the presidential system?
o: Fresh elections to break a deadlock
x: Stability of a fixed-term executive is the presidential merit; the other three are merits of the parliamentary system.

s: According to Dr B.R. Ambedkar, which two things can a democracy not maximise together?
x: Ambedkar said a democracy cannot maximise stability and responsibility together, so the parliamentary form does not guarantee both.

s: From working which Acts did the Constituent Assembly gain familiarity with parliamentary government?
x: Familiarity under the Government of India Acts of 1919 and 1935 was one reason for choosing the parliamentary form.

s: According to Dr B.R. Ambedkar, to what did India's choice of government give greater weight?
o: Responsibility and continuous accountability over guaranteed tenure
x: Dr B.R. Ambedkar observed that a democracy cannot maximise both stability and responsibility. India chose responsibility, meaning continuous accountability, over guaranteed tenure.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Vasant Sathe — proposals for a presidential form in the 1970s–80s
Venkatachaliah Commission — recommendation to replace parliamentary government with a presidential system
One Nation, One Election — amendment only to Article 74
Dr B.R. Ambedkar — advocacy of guaranteed executive tenure over accountability
x: Vasant Sathe was associated with proposals for a presidential form of government in India during the 1970s–80s. The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution advised retaining the parliamentary system, while the relevant One Nation, One Election proposal concerns Articles 83, 172 and 327.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Shamsher Singh (1974)?
o: It is relevant to the limits parliamentary responsibility places on constitutional office-holders
It connected the Governor's conduct with the logic of the parliamentary system
It held public criticism of Cabinet policy by the Governor compatible with parliamentary conventions
x: Public criticism of Cabinet policy by the Governor was held to run counter to the parliamentary system.

s: The One Nation, One Election proposal involves amendments to which Articles?
x: One Nation, One Election amends Articles 83, 172 and 327; critics say fixed tenures graft presidential mechanics onto the system.

s: Who proposed a presidential form of government for India in the 1970s-80s?
x: Vasant Sathe proposed a presidential form; the NCRWC under Venkatachaliah advised keeping the parliamentary system.

s: What did the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (2000-02) advise about India's form of government?
o: Have a directly elected Prime Minister
x: The NCRWC headed by M.N. Venkatachaliah advised keeping the parliamentary system.
